books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Stephen A. Douglas, Freeport debate answer (August 27, 1858)

stimulus.source_note: Stephen A. Douglas, answer at the Freeport debate, August 27, 1858 (second Lincoln-Douglas debate). Public domain. Wording verified against the debate text (Britannica, Freeport Doctrine; National Park Service, Lincoln Home).
stimulus.text: It matters not what way the Supreme Court may hereafter decide as to the abstract question whether slavery may or may not go into a Territory under the Constitution, the people have the lawful means to introduce it or exclude it as they please, for the reason that slavery cannot exist a day or an hour anywhere, unless it is supported by local police regulations.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Douglas’s Freeport answer most directly cost him support among

options.text: Illinois voters, who had rejected popular sovereignty.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Douglas kept his Senate seat in 1858; Illinois voters returned him.

options.text: Southern Democrats, who wanted slavery protected in the territories.
Republicans, who had backed the Dred Scott decision.
options.misconception: The Republicans attacked the Dred Scott decision; Douglas’s answer did not cost him their support, since he never had it.

options.text: Northern workers, who feared competition from free Black labor.
options.misconception: Northern workers backed Douglas’s popular sovereignty; the doctrine cost him Southern, not Northern, friends.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Douglas kept his Senate seat in 1858; Illinois voters returned him.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Southern Democrats demanded slavery be protected in the territories, and the Freeport Doctrine let territories refuse that protection.
rationales.C: The Republicans attacked the Dred Scott decision; Douglas’s answer did not cost him their support, since he never had it.
rationales.D: Northern workers backed Douglas’s popular sovereignty; the doctrine cost him Southern, not Northern, friends.
rationales.general:
1. Read the doctrine: a territory can keep slavery out by refusing it police protection.
2. Ask who hates that: Southern Democrats, who wanted federal protection for slavery everywhere.
3. See the cost: Douglas won Illinois and lost the South, splitting his party before 1860.
Remember: an answer that saves you at home can ruin you with the rest of your party.
